items.title: View Changes (git diff)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git diff shows the differences between versions of your files.
For beginners, the most important thing to understand is:
Modify a file ↓ git diff ↓ See what changed since the last saved/staged state
By default, git diff shows unstaged changes — changes in your Working Directory that have not yet been added to the Staging Area.
Simple Rule: git diff helps you see exactly what you changed before creating a commit.
Why Do We Need git diff?
Imagine you modify a file several times. After some time, you may forget exactly what you changed.
Original file ↓ Make change 1 ↓ Make change 2 ↓ Make change 3 ↓ Forget what changed 🤔 ↓ git diff ↓ See the differences ✅
This is useful before staging or committing your changes.
Basic Command
git diff
Run this command inside your Git repository.
Git compares your current unstaged file changes with the version Git is currently using as the comparison point for unstaged changes.
At this stage, remember the simple workflow:
File changed in Working Directory ↓ git diff ↓ View unstaged changes
Simple Example
Suppose your index.html file was previously saved in a commit like this:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
Now you modify it:
<h1>Welcome</h1> <p>Learn Git and GitHub</p>
Before using git add, run:
git diff
Git can show output similar to:
- <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h1>Welcome</h1> + <p>Learn Git and GitHub</p>
The important symbol here is:

SymbolMeaning
-Removed line from the compared version
+Added line in the new version
Do not worry about memorizing the complete diff output format yet. First understand that git diff shows what was added, removed, or changed.
Understanding Added and Removed Lines
Suppose the original file contains:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
You change it to:
<h1>Welcome to My Website</h1>
The diff may show something similar to:
- <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h1>Welcome to My Website</h1>
Git treats this as one line removed and one line added.
Old version - Welcome New version + Welcome to My Website
Where Does git diff Fit in the Git Workflow?
You have already learned the main Git working areas:
Working Directory ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository
git diff is mainly used to inspect differences between these states.
For now, focus on the default command:
Working Directory Modified changes ↓ git diff ↓ See unstaged changes
Important: git diff Does Not Change Anything
git diff is a viewing command. It does not modify your files.
git diff ↓ Only displays differences 👀 Does NOT: ├── Modify files ├── Stage files ├── Create commits ├── Delete commits └── Upload to GitHub
You can safely run git diff whenever you want to inspect changes.
git diff Before git add
A common workflow is to review your changes before staging them.
1. Modify file ↓ 2. git status ↓ 3. git diff ↓ 4. Review changes ↓ 5. git add ↓ 6. git commit
This helps you check whether the changes are correct before adding them to the Staging Area.
Example Workflow
Suppose you add a new heading to index.html.
index.html Original version: <h1>Welcome</h1> ↓ You modify the file: <h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Git Learning Roadmap</h2>
Now check the repository:
git status
Then inspect the actual changes:
git diff
After confirming the change is correct:
git add index.html git commit -m "Add Git roadmap heading"
What Happens After git add?
This is an important concept.
Suppose you modify index.html and run:
git add index.html
The changes move to the Staging Area.
If you now run the normal command:
git diff
You may see no output for those staged changes because the default git diff command focuses on unstaged changes.
Modify file ↓ git diff ↓ See changes ✅ ↓ git add index.html ↓ Changes become staged ↓ git diff ↓ Staged changes are not shown by default
In the next related topic, you will learn how to view staged changes using:
git diff --staged
Very Important: git diff vs git diff --staged
These commands inspect different areas.

CommandShows
git diffUnstaged changes in the Working Directory
git diff --stagedChanges currently in the Staging Area
Working Directory Modified but not staged ↓ git diff -------------------- git add ↓ Staging Area Ready for commit ↓ git diff --staged
You will study git diff --staged in more detail in Topic 23.
What If You Modify a File and git diff Shows Nothing?
One possible reason is that you already staged the changes.
Modify file ↓ git add file ↓ Changes are staged ↓ git diff ↓ No output for those staged changes
In that situation, check:
git status
Then view the staged changes with:
git diff --staged
What If You Have Multiple Modified Files?
git diff can show unstaged differences from multiple modified files.
Working Directory │ ├── index.html → Modified ├── style.css → Modified └── script.js → Modified ↓ git diff ↓ View differences from all unstaged files
If you want to inspect one specific file, you can use:
git diff index.html
This is useful when a project contains many changes and you want to focus on one file.
Common Beginner Confusion: git diff vs git status
Both commands help you inspect your work, but they answer different questions.

CommandMain Question
git statusWhich files have changed and what state are they in?
git diffWhat exactly changed inside the files?
git status → WHICH files changed? -------------------- git diff → WHAT changed inside them?
Example: status + diff Together
Suppose you modify two files.
index.html → Add heading style.css → Change font size
Run:
git status
Git tells you that the files were modified.
Then run:
git diff
Git shows the actual lines that changed.
git status ↓ index.html → Modified style.css → Modified ↓ Need exact details? ↓ git diff ↓ See changed lines
git diff Helps Before Committing
Before committing, reviewing your changes can help you catch mistakes.
Make changes ↓ git diff ↓ Review carefully ↓ Correct mistakes if needed ↓ git add ↓ git commit
This is especially useful when you made many changes and want to verify what will eventually be included in your project history.
Example of Finding a Mistake
Suppose you intended to change:
<h1>Git Roadmap</h1>
But you accidentally wrote:
<h1>Gti Roadmap</h1>
Running git diff can help you notice the incorrect change:
- Git Roadmap + Gti Roadmap ❌ ↓ Notice mistake ↓ Fix file ↓ Run git diff again ↓ Correct change ✅
Simple Comparison of Current Topics

CommandPurpose
git statusCheck current file and staging state
git addStage changes
git commitSave staged changes in local history
git logView previous commits
git diffView exact unstaged changes
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git status → What files changed? ↓ git diff → What changed inside the files? ↓ git add → Select changes ↓ git commit → Save changes
Complete Flow

Modify index.html ↓ git status ↓ See that index.html changed ↓ git diff ↓ See exactly what changed ↓ git add index.html ↓ Move changes to Staging Area ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage heading" ↓ Save in Local Repository ✅
One-Line Definition: git diff displays the exact differences in your files, and by default it is commonly used to view unstaged changes in the Working Directory.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository. First make sure you have at least one committed version of index.html.
STEP 1 → Open index.html ↓ STEP 2 → Make a small change ↓ STEP 3 → Run git status ↓ STEP 4 → Run git diff ↓ STEP 5 → Observe the changed lines
For example, add a new heading to index.html and save the file.
<h2>Learning Git Diff</h2>
Now check which file changed:
git status
Then view exactly what changed inside the file:
git diff
git status ↓ index.html → Modified ↓ git diff ↓ - Old content + New content
Do not run git add immediately. First carefully observe the output from git diff and identify the line you added or changed.
Next: Stage the file and compare the behavior.
git add index.html git status git diff
Notice that the normal git diff may no longer show the staged change. This happens because the change is now in the Staging Area.
Now view the staged change:
git diff --staged
Before git add ↓ git diff Shows unstaged change ✅ After git add ↓ git diff Does not show that staged change by default ↓ git diff --staged Shows staged change ✅
Finally, commit your change with a meaningful message.
git commit -m "Add Git diff practice heading"
Practice Goal: Clearly understand the difference between git status (which files changed), git diff (what changed), and git diff --staged (what is currently staged).

qna.q: Q1. What does git diff do?
qna.a: git diff displays the differences between versions of your files and is commonly used to inspect exact changes.

qna.q: Q2. What does git diff show by default?
qna.a: By default, git diff shows unstaged changes in the Working Directory.

qna.q: Q3. What is the difference between git status and git diff?
qna.a: git status shows which files changed and their current state, while git diff shows the exact content changes inside the files.

qna.q: Q4. Does git diff modify your files?
qna.a: No. git diff only displays differences and does not modify your files.

qna.q: Q5. What does a + symbol usually represent in git diff output?
qna.a: It represents a line that was added in the new version.

qna.q: Q6. What does a - symbol usually represent in git diff output?
qna.a: It represents a line from the compared version that was removed or replaced.

qna.q: Q7. What usually happens when you run git diff after staging all your changes?
qna.a: The normal git diff command may show no output for those changes because they are now staged.

qna.q: Q8. Which command can be used to view staged changes?
qna.a: git diff --staged

qna.q: Q9. Can git diff help you find mistakes before committing?
qna.a: Yes. It allows you to review the exact changes and correct mistakes before staging or committing them.

qna.q: Q10. What is the recommended basic workflow before committing a change?
qna.a: Modify files → git status → git diff → review changes → git add → git commit.

items.title: Modified vs Staged vs Committed
explanation: Simple Meaning
When working with Git, your changes can exist in different states. The three most important states are Modified, Staged, and Committed.
Modify a file ↓ Modified ↓ git add ↓ Staged ↓ git commit ↓ Committed
Simple Rule: Modified means you changed a file. Staged means you selected the change for the next commit. Committed means the change was saved in your local Git history.
The Complete Journey of a Change
Suppose your repository already contains index.html. You edit the file and add a new heading.
Original committed version ↓ Edit index.html ↓ Modified ↓ git add index.html ↓ Staged ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage heading" ↓ Committed
These are not three different copies of your file. They describe the state of your changes during the Git workflow.
1. What Is Modified?
A file is Modified when you change it after the last committed version, but the new changes have not yet been staged.
Example: Your committed index.html contains:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
You change it to:
<h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Learn Git</h2>
After saving the file, Git sees that the file has changed.
Local Repository Last committed version ↓ You edit index.html ↓ Working Directory index.html → Modified ✏️
You can check this using:
git status
Modified Means: Changes Exist in the Working Directory
Working Directory │ └── index.html Modified ✏️ The change is: Not staged yet ❌ Not committed yet ❌
At this stage, you have changed the file, but you have not told Git to include that change in the next commit.
2. What Is Staged?
A change becomes Staged when you use git add to select it for the next commit.
For example:
git add index.html
Now the current version of that change is placed in the Staging Area.
Working Directory Modified change ↓ git add index.html ↓ Staging Area Change selected for next commit 📦
Staged does not mean committed. The change is ready to be committed, but it has not yet been saved in Git history.
Staged Means: Ready for the Next Commit
Working Directory ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area index.html → Staged 📦 Ready for next commit Not committed yet ⏳
You can use git status to see which changes are staged.
3. What Is Committed?
A change becomes Committed when you run git commit and Git records the staged snapshot in the local repository history.
Example:
git commit -m "Add homepage heading"
Staging Area Change ready ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository ↓ Commit created ✅ ↓ Change saved in Git history
Now the change is part of your local Git history.
Committed Does Not Mean Uploaded to GitHub
This is a very important concept.
git commit ↓ Saved in Local Repository ✅ GitHub updated automatically? ❌
A commit is created locally on your computer. Uploading commits to GitHub is a separate action that you will learn later using git push.
Simple Example Using One File
Let's follow index.html through all three states.
Step 1: The file was already committed.
Local Repository Commit 1 index.html <h1>Welcome</h1>
Step 2: You change the file.
<h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Git Learning</h2>
State → Modified ✏️
Step 3: You stage the change.
git add index.html
State → Staged 📦
Step 4: You commit the staged change.
git commit -m "Add Git learning heading"
State → Committed ✅
Visualizing the Three Git States
The Commands That Move Changes

Current StateCommandNext State
Modifiedgit addStaged
Stagedgit commitCommitted
Modified │ │ git add ↓ Staged │ │ git commit ↓ Committed
How git status Shows These States
git status helps you understand where your changes currently are.
If you modify a file but do not stage it, Git can show it as modified.
Changes not staged for commit: modified: index.html State → Modified ✏️
After running git add index.html, Git can show the file under changes ready to be committed.
Changes to be committed: new file: index.html or modified: index.html State → Staged 📦
After committing, there are no longer uncommitted changes from that snapshot.
git status ↓ nothing to commit, working tree clean Latest changes → Committed ✅
Modified vs Staged

ModifiedStaged
You changed the fileYou selected the change for the next commit
Exists in Working DirectoryRecorded in Staging Area
Not ready as the staged snapshotReady for the next commit
View with git diffView with git diff --staged
Move using git addSave using git commit
Staged vs Committed

StagedCommitted
Selected for the next commitAlready saved in Git history
Exists in the Staging AreaExists as a commit in Local Repository
Can still be changed before committingAlready recorded as a history entry
Use git commit to save itView history with git log
Modified vs Committed

ModifiedCommitted
Current unsaved Git changeRecorded Git history snapshot
Not yet staged or committedAlready saved locally
Can be inspected with git diffCan be viewed in history with git log
Very Important Example: Stage Only One File
Suppose you modify two files:
index.html → Modified ✏️ style.css → Modified ✏️
Now you run:
git add index.html
The states become:
index.html → Staged 📦 style.css → Still Modified ✏️
Now run:
git commit -m "Update homepage"
Only the staged change is included in the commit.
index.html → Committed ✅ style.css → Still Modified ✏️
Important: Git allows different files to be in different states at the same time.
Another Important Example: Modify a File Again After Staging
This is an important Git concept.
Suppose you modify index.html:
Modify index.html ↓ Modified ✏️
You stage it:
git add index.html
index.html → Staged 📦
Then you edit index.html again without running git add again.
Staged version → Version A 📦 Working Directory → Version B ✏️
Now the Staging Area contains the earlier staged snapshot, while your newer changes remain modified in the Working Directory.
Important: If you make more changes after git add, run git add again if you want the newer changes included in the next commit.
Example of the Same File in Two States
Step 1 Modify index.html ↓ Step 2 git add index.html ↓ Staged Version A 📦 ↓ Step 3 Modify index.html again ↓ Staging Area → Version A 📦 Working Directory → New Version B ✏️
If you commit now, Git commits the staged Version A. The newer Version B changes remain modified unless you stage them too.
Complete Example Workflow
Suppose you add a navigation bar to your website.

STEP 1 Edit index.html Add navigation bar ↓ State → Modified ✏️ ↓ STEP 2 Run git status Confirm file is modified ↓ STEP 3 Run git diff Review exact changes ↓ STEP 4 Run git add index.html ↓ State → Staged 📦 ↓ STEP 5 Run git diff --staged Review staged changes ↓ STEP 6 Run git commit -m "Add navigation bar" ↓ State → Committed ✅
All Three States Together

StateMeaningLocationMain Command
ModifiedYou changed the fileWorking Directorygit diff
StagedSelected for next commitStaging Areagit add
CommittedSaved in Git historyLocal Repositorygit log
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Modified ✏️ "I changed it" ↓ git add ↓ Staged 📦 "I selected it for the next commit" ↓ git commit ↓ Committed ✅ "Git saved it in history"
Connection With Previous Topics

Topic 16 → git status Shows current states Topic 17 → git add Moves selected changes to Staging Area Topic 18 → git commit Saves staged changes in Local Repository Topic 20 → git log Shows committed history Topic 21 → git diff Shows exact unstaged changes Topic 22 → You now understand how these states connect ✅

One-Line Definition: Modified means a file has been changed in the Working Directory, Staged means the change has been selected in the Staging Area for the next commit, and Committed means the staged change has been saved as a commit in the local Git repository.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository and follow the complete journey of one file.
STEP 1 → Modify a file ↓ Observe → Modified ✏️ ↓ STEP 2 → Stage the file ↓ Observe → Staged 📦 ↓ STEP 3 → Commit the file ↓ Observe → Committed ✅
Step 1: Open index.html, add a small heading, and save the file.
<h2>Modified Staged Committed Practice</h2>
Now check its state:
git status
Expected state: index.html → Modified ✏️
View exactly what changed:
git diff
Step 2: Stage the file.
git add index.html
Check the state again:
git status
Expected state: index.html → Staged 📦 Ready for the next commit
View the staged version:
git diff --staged
Step 3: Commit the staged change.
git commit -m "Add Git states practice heading"
Now check the repository:
git status
Expected result: Working tree clean ↓ Latest change committed ✅
Finally, confirm that the commit exists in your history:
git log
Modify ↓ Modified ✏️ ↓ git add ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ git commit ↓ Committed ✅ ↓ git log ↓ See the commit in history
Extra Practice: Modify both index.html and style.css, but stage only index.html. Run git status and observe that Git can show one file as staged while the other remains modified.
index.html → Modify + git add ↓ Staged 📦 style.css → Modify only ↓ Modified ✏️ Both states can exist at the same time ✅
Practice Goal: You should clearly understand this journey: I change a file → Modified. I run git add → Staged. I run git commit → Committed in local history.

qna.q: Q1. What does Modified mean in Git?
qna.a: Modified means you changed a file in the Working Directory, but the change has not yet been staged for the next commit.

qna.q: Q2. What does Staged mean in Git?
qna.a: Staged means the change has been selected and placed in the Staging Area for the next commit.

qna.q: Q3. What does Committed mean in Git?
qna.a: Committed means the staged change has been recorded as a commit in the local Git repository history.

qna.q: Q4. Which command moves a modified change to the Staging Area?
qna.a: git add

qna.q: Q5. Which command saves staged changes in the Local Repository?
qna.a: git commit

qna.q: Q6. Which command can show the exact unstaged changes?
qna.a: git diff

qna.q: Q7. Which command can show the exact staged changes?
qna.a: git diff --staged

qna.q: Q8. Can two files be in different Git states at the same time?
qna.a: Yes. For example, index.html can be staged while style.css remains modified.

qna.q: Q9. After running git add on a file, is it automatically committed?
qna.a: No. git add only stages the change. You still need to run git commit to save it in Git history.

qna.q: Q10. You stage index.html and then modify it again. Will the new modification automatically be included in the next commit?
qna.a: No. The newer modification must be staged again with git add if you want that newer version included in the next commit.

items.title: View Staged Changes (git diff --staged)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git diff --staged shows the changes that are currently in the Staging Area and will be included in your next commit.
Modify a file ↓ git add ↓ Changes enter Staging Area 📦 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ See what will be committed
Simple Rule: git diff shows unstaged changes, while git diff --staged shows staged changes.
Why Do We Need It?
Before creating a commit, you may want to check exactly what you staged.
Make changes ↓ git add ↓ Changes are staged ↓ Did I stage the correct changes? 🤔 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Review before committing ✅

This helps you verify the contents of your next commit before running git commit. Git documents --staged as a synonym for --cached; it compares the staged changes with the last commit by default. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0}
Basic Command
git diff --staged
You can also use:
git diff --cached
Both commands mean the same thing for viewing changes staged for the next commit. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1}
Where Does It Fit in the Git Workflow?
Working Directory Modify file ✏️ ↓ git diff ↓ View unstaged changes ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area 📦 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ View staged changes ↓ git commit ↓ Local Repository ✅
The main purpose is simple: use it to inspect the changes you have already selected for the next commit.
Simple Example
Suppose your last committed index.html contains:
<h1>Welcome</h1>
Now you change it to:
<h1>Welcome</h1> <h2>Learning Git</h2>
First, the file is modified. Run:
git diff
You can see the unstaged change.
Now stage it:
git add index.html
The change is now staged. Run:
git diff --staged
You can now see the exact change currently prepared for the next commit.
Example Output
The output may look similar to this:
- <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h1>Welcome</h1> + <h2>Learning Git</h2>
The important symbols are:

SymbolMeaning
-Line removed from the previous committed version
+Line added in the staged version
git diff vs git diff --staged
This is the most important comparison for this topic.

CommandShows
git diffChanges not yet staged
git diff --stagedChanges staged for the next commit
Working Directory Modified but not staged ✏️ ↓ git diff ==================== git add ↓ Staging Area Staged for commit 📦 ↓ git diff --staged

Git's documentation specifically describes git diff as comparing unstaged working-tree changes with the staging area, while git diff --staged shows what has been staged relative to the last commit. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2}
Important: What Happens After git add?
Suppose you make a change and then run:
git add index.html
The change moves into the Staging Area.
Before git add ↓ Modified ✏️ ↓ git diff Shows change ✅ After git add ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ git diff Usually no longer shows that staged change ↓ git diff --staged Shows staged change ✅
If all your changes are staged, running plain git diff can produce no output because it only shows changes that are still unstaged. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3}
View What Will Be in the Next Commit
This is an easy way to remember the command:
git diff --staged ↓ "What have I prepared for my next commit?"
If you run:
git commit -m "My commit message"
Git records the currently staged snapshot. Therefore, checking git diff --staged before committing helps you review that snapshot. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4}
Example With Two Files
Suppose you modify two files:
index.html → Modified ✏️ style.css → Modified ✏️
Now stage only one file:
git add index.html
The states are now:
index.html → Staged 📦 style.css → Modified ✏️
Run:
git diff
This shows the unstaged changes in style.css.
Run:
git diff --staged
This shows the staged changes in index.html.
git diff ↓ style.css changes ✏️ -------------------- git diff --staged ↓ index.html changes 📦
Using git status Together With git diff --staged
A useful workflow is:
git status git diff --staged
git status tells you which files are staged, while git diff --staged shows the exact content changes. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5}
git status ↓ Which files are staged? ↓ git diff --staged ↓ What exactly changed inside them?
Important Example: Modify Again After Staging
Suppose you modify index.html and stage it:
Modify Version A ↓ git add index.html ↓ Version A is Staged 📦
Then you edit the same file again:
Staging Area → Version A 📦 Working Directory → Version B ✏️
Now run:
git diff
You see the newer unstaged difference between the Working Directory and the Staging Area.
Then run:
git diff --staged
You see the previously staged Version A compared with the last commit.

Important: git add stages the content as it exists when you run the command. If you change the file again and want those newer changes in the next commit, you need to run git add again. :contentReference[oaicite:6]{index=6}
Visual Example of the Same File

Last Commit Version 0 ↓ Modify file ↓ Version A ↓ git add ↓ Staging Area → Version A 📦 ↓ Modify file again ↓ Working Directory → Version B ✏️ Now: git diff → Shows B compared with staged A git diff --staged → Shows staged A compared with committed version 0
Why Review Staged Changes Before Commit?
Sometimes you may accidentally stage the wrong file or an unfinished change.
Modify many files ↓ git add files ↓ Something unnecessary may be staged 😬 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Review changes ↓ Correct staging if needed ↓ git commit
Reviewing staged changes before committing is a good habit, especially as projects become larger.
Compare the Main Commands You Learned

CommandMain Purpose
git statusSee the current state of files
git diffSee exact unstaged changes
git addStage selected changes
git diff --stagedSee exact staged changes
git commitSave staged changes in local history
Complete Workflow

1. Edit index.html ↓ Modified ✏️ ↓ 2. git status ↓ See modified file ↓ 3. git diff ↓ Review unstaged changes ↓ 4. git add index.html ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ 5. git diff --staged ↓ Review what will be committed ↓ 6. git commit -m "Add homepage heading" ↓ Committed in Local Repository ✅
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git diff → "What changed but I have NOT staged?" -------------------- git diff --staged → "What DID I stage for my next commit?"
One-Line Definition: git diff --staged displays the exact changes currently staged for the next commit, typically by comparing the Staging Area with the latest commit.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository. Make sure your previous work is committed before starting.
STEP 1 → Modify index.html ↓ STEP 2 → Run git diff ↓ STEP 3 → Run git add ↓ STEP 4 → Run git diff --staged ↓ STEP 5 → Compare both commands ↓ STEP 6 → Commit
Step 1: Open index.html, add a small heading, and save the file.
<h2>Learning Staged Changes</h2>
Step 2: Check the exact unstaged change.
git status git diff
Current state: index.html → Modified ✏️ Command: git diff ↓ Shows the new heading
Step 3: Stage the file.
git add index.html
Step 4: Check the file state again.
git status
Current state: index.html → Staged 📦 Ready for the next commit
Step 5: Now run both commands separately and observe the difference.
git diff git diff --staged
git diff ↓ No output for the fully staged change -------------------- git diff --staged ↓ Shows the staged change ✅
Step 6: Modify the same file again after staging it. For example, add another line:
<p>This change is made after staging.</p>
Now run:
git diff git diff --staged
git diff ↓ Shows the NEW unstaged change ✏️ -------------------- git diff --staged ↓ Shows the EARLIER staged change 📦
This is the most important practice in this topic. It demonstrates that the Working Directory and Staging Area can contain different versions of the same file.
Step 7: If you want the newer change included in the commit, stage the file again.
git add index.html
Review the complete staged version:
git diff --staged
Step 8: Commit the changes.
git commit -m "Practice viewing staged changes"
Modified ✏️ ↓ git diff ↓ Staged 📦 ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Modify again ✏️ ↓ Working Directory and Staging Area differ ↓ git add again ↓ Review staged changes ↓ git commit ✅
Practice Goal: Clearly understand that git diff shows unstaged changes, while git diff --staged shows the changes currently prepared for your next commit.

qna.q: Q1. What does git diff --staged do?
qna.a: It shows the exact changes currently in the Staging Area that are prepared for the next commit.

qna.q: Q2. What is the difference between git diff and git diff --staged?
qna.a: git diff shows unstaged changes, while git diff --staged shows staged changes.

qna.q: Q3. Which command should you use to review what will be included in your next commit?
qna.a: git diff --staged

qna.q: Q4. Is git diff --staged the same as git diff --cached?
qna.a: Yes. --staged and --cached are synonyms for this purpose.

qna.q: Q5. What does git diff --staged typically compare by default?
qna.a: It compares the staged changes with the latest commit, also known as HEAD.

qna.q: Q6. If you stage all changes and run plain git diff, why might you see no output?
qna.a: Because plain git diff shows unstaged changes, and the changes have already been moved to the Staging Area.

qna.q: Q7. You run git add index.html and then modify index.html again. What does git diff --staged show?
qna.a: It shows the version that was staged when git add was run, compared with the last commit. The newer modification remains unstaged.

qna.q: Q8. If you modify a file after staging it, how do you include the new modification in the next commit?
qna.a: Run git add again after making the newer modification.

qna.q: Q9. Does git diff --staged create a commit?
qna.a: No. It only displays staged changes. You must run git commit to create a commit.

qna.q: Q10. What is a good workflow before committing?
qna.a: Modify files → git diff → git add → git diff --staged → review → git commit.

items.title: View Commit History (git log)
explanation: Simple Meaning
The command git log shows the history of commits in your Git repository.
Every time you run git commit, Git creates a new entry in the repository history. git log allows you to view those entries.
Commit 1 → Create project ↓ Commit 2 → Add login page ↓ Commit 3 → Add dashboard ↓ Commit 4 → Fix login bug ↓ git log ↓ View complete commit history 📜
Simple Rule: git commit creates history. git log shows that history.
Why Do We Need Commit History?
As your project grows, you may create many commits. Later, you may want to know what happened in the project.
Questions you may have: What changes were made? 🤔 Who created a commit? 👤 When was it created? 📅 What was the commit message? 💬 What is the commit ID? 🔑 ↓ git log ↓ Get commit history ✅
Commit history is one of the main reasons Git is useful because it creates a timeline of your project's development.
Basic Command
git log
Run this command inside a Git repository.
Git displays commits from the current branch, usually showing the newest commit first.
Newest Commit ↓ Commit 3 ↓ Commit 2 ↓ Commit 1 ↓ Oldest Commit
Simple Example
Suppose you create three commits:
git commit -m "Create project" git commit -m "Add login page" git commit -m "Add dashboard"
Now run:
git log
You may see output similar to:

commit a1b2c3d4e5f6... Author: Nethaji Date: Mon Sep 1 10:30:00 2026 +0530 Add dashboard commit b2c3d4e5f6a7... Author: Nethaji Date: Mon Sep 1 10:00:00 2026 +0530 Add login page commit c3d4e5f6a7b8... Author: Nethaji Date: Mon Sep 1 09:30:00 2026 +0530 Create project
The actual commit IDs, author names, and dates on your computer will be different.
Understanding git log Output
A normal git log entry contains several important pieces of information.
commit a1b2c3d4... ↓ Commit ID Author: Nethaji ↓ Who created the commit Date: Mon Sep 1... ↓ When the commit was created Add dashboard ↓ Commit message
1. Commit ID
Every commit has a unique identifier called a commit hash or commit ID.
commit a1b2c3d4e5f6...
The real commit ID is a long hexadecimal value. Git often allows you to use a shorter unique beginning portion when referring to a commit.
For now, remember:
Every Commit ↓ Has a unique ID 🔑 ↓ Used to identify that specific commit
2. Author
The Author field shows the name and email associated with the person who created the commit.
Author: Nethaji
This connects with the Git username and email configuration you learned earlier.
git config user.name ↓ Git records author information ↓ git commit ↓ Commit history shows author
3. Date
The Date field shows when the commit was created.
Date: Mon Sep 1 10:30:00 2026 +0530
This helps you understand the order and timeline of project changes.
4. Commit Message
The commit message explains the purpose of the commit.
Add dashboard
Good commit messages make the history easier to understand.
Bad history ❌ Update Changes Fixed Test -------------------- Clear history ✅ Create project Add login page Add dashboard Fix login validation
Commit History as a Project Timeline
You can think of git log as the timeline of your project.
Day 1 Commit → Create website ↓ Day 2 Commit → Add navigation ↓ Day 3 Commit → Add login page ↓ Day 4 Commit → Fix login validation ↓ Day 5 Run git log ↓ See project history 📜
git log vs git status
These commands answer different questions.

CommandMain Question
git statusWhat is happening right now?
git logWhat happened in previous commits?
git status ↓ Current state Modified? Staged? Clean? ==================== git log ↓ Previous history What commits were created?
git log vs git diff

CommandPurpose
git diffView changes that have not yet been committed
git logView commits that already exist in history
Current uncommitted changes ↓ git diff ==================== Already committed changes ↓ git log
Important: git log Shows Commits, Not Current Uncommitted Changes
Suppose you have this situation:
Commit 1 → Create index.html Commit 2 → Add login page ↓ You now modify index.html But do NOT commit it yet
If you run:
git log
You will see Commit 1 and Commit 2, but your new uncommitted modification will not appear as a new commit in the history.
Uncommitted change ✏️ ↓ git diff / git status Committed history 📜 ↓ git log
View a Shorter History with git log --oneline
Normal git log can display many details. For a shorter view, use:
git log --oneline
Example output:
a1b2c3d Add dashboard b2c3d4e Add login page c3d4e5f Create project
This usually shows a shortened commit ID and the commit message on one line.
Normal git log ↓ Detailed information -------------------- git log --oneline ↓ Short commit history
Why git log --oneline Is Useful
When your repository has many commits, the shorter view makes it easier to quickly understand the history.
a1b2c3d Add dashboard b2c3d4e Add login page c3d4e5f Create project Quick project timeline ✅
You will often use git log --oneline when you want a quick overview.
Viewing the Latest Few Commits
You can limit the number of commits displayed using:
git log -n 3
This displays the latest three commits.
You can change the number:
git log -n 5
git log -n 3 ↓ Latest 3 commits -------------------- git log -n 5 ↓ Latest 5 commits
Useful Combination: --oneline with a Limit
You can combine options:
git log --oneline -n 5
This gives a compact view of the latest five commits.
Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message Short Commit ID → Commit Message
Understanding HEAD in the History
When you run git log, you may see something like:
commit a1b2c3d4... (HEAD -> main)
For now, understand this simply:
HEAD ↓ Points to your current commit
If you are currently working on the main branch, HEAD -> main means your current position is at the latest commit of that branch.
You will understand branches and HEAD in greater detail later in the branching section.
Complete Example
Suppose you perform these actions:

Create project ↓ git commit -m "Create project" ↓ Add index.html ↓ git commit -m "Add homepage" ↓ Add style.css ↓ git commit -m "Add website styles" ↓ Fix a CSS issue ↓ git commit -m "Fix navigation styling"
Now run:
git log --oneline
You may see:
f4e5d6c Fix navigation styling c3d4e5f Add website styles b2c3d4e Add homepage a1b2c3d Create project
The newest commit appears first, followed by older commits.
Useful Commands for Viewing History

CommandPurpose
git logView detailed commit history
git log --onelineView compact commit history
git log -n 3View latest 3 commits
git log --oneline -n 5View compact latest 5 commits
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
git status → What is happening NOW? -------------------- git diff → What changed but is not committed? -------------------- git log → What has ALREADY been committed?
Complete Git Flow So Far

Modify file ↓ git status ↓ Check current state ↓ git diff ↓ Review unstaged changes ↓ git add ↓ Stage changes ↓ git diff --staged ↓ Review staged changes ↓ git commit ↓ Create commit ↓ git log ↓ View commit history 📜
One-Line Definition: git log displays the commit history of a Git repository, allowing you to view previous commits, their IDs, authors, dates, and commit messages.
practice: Use your Git-Practice repository. Make sure you have at least 3 commits before starting this practice.
STEP 1 → Create or confirm multiple commits ↓ STEP 2 → Run git log ↓ STEP 3 → Identify commit details ↓ STEP 4 → Run git log --oneline ↓ STEP 5 → Compare detailed and compact history
Step 1: First check your current commit history.
git log
Look at each commit and try to identify:
Commit ID 🔑 Author 👤 Date 📅 Commit Message 💬
Step 2: Now view the same history in a shorter format.
git log --oneline
Compare the output with normal git log.
git log ↓ Detailed history ==================== git log --oneline ↓ Short history Same commits Different amount of detail
Step 3: View only the latest three commits.
git log -n 3
Check whether exactly three commits are displayed.
Step 4: Try a compact view of the latest two commits.
git log --oneline -n 2
Latest commit ↓ Previous commit Only 2 commits displayed ✅
Step 5: Make one small change to index.html, but do not stage or commit it.
<p>This change is not committed yet.</p>
Now run these commands:
git status git diff git log --oneline
git status → Shows current modified file -------------------- git diff → Shows exact uncommitted change -------------------- git log --oneline → Does NOT show the change as a new commit
This is important: a change appears in commit history only after it is staged and committed.
Final Step: Stage and commit the change.
git add index.html git commit -m "Add commit history practice text"
Now run:
git log --oneline
Before commit ↓ New change not in history ❌ After git commit ↓ New commit appears in history ✅
Practice Goal: Clearly understand that git log shows committed history, git log --oneline gives a compact history, and uncommitted changes do not appear as commits until you run git commit.

qna.q: Q1. What does git log do?
qna.a: git log displays the commit history of the current Git repository.

qna.q: Q2. Which command creates a new entry in Git history?
qna.a: git commit creates a new commit in Git history.

qna.q: Q3. What information can normal git log display?
qna.a: It can display information such as the commit ID, author, date, and commit message.

qna.q: Q4. Does git log show uncommitted changes as commits?
qna.a: No. git log shows commits that already exist in the repository history. Uncommitted changes do not appear as new commits.

qna.q: Q5. In what order are commits usually shown by git log?
qna.a: The newest commits are usually shown first, followed by older commits.

qna.q: Q6. What does git log --oneline do?
qna.a: It shows a compact version of commit history, usually with a shortened commit ID and commit message on each line.

qna.q: Q7. Which command can show only the latest three commits?
qna.a: git log -n 3

qna.q: Q8. What is a commit ID?
qna.a: A commit ID, also called a commit hash, is a unique identifier used to identify a specific commit.

qna.q: Q9. What is the difference between git status and git log?
qna.a: git status shows the current state of your working files, while git log shows the history of commits that were already created.

qna.q: Q10. What is the difference between git diff and git log?
qna.a: git diff is used to inspect changes that have not yet been committed, while git log is used to view commits already saved in repository history.

items.title: What is a Branch?
explanation: Simple Meaning
A branch in Git is an independent line of development. It allows you to work on changes without directly affecting the main line of your project.
main ↓ Project working code ✅ Create a branch ↓ feature-login ↓ Work on login feature separately
Simple Definition: A branch is a separate line of development where you can make changes independently.
Why Do We Need Branches?
Imagine your website is working correctly on the main branch.
main ↓ Website working perfectly ✅
Now you want to add a new login feature. The feature may take several days and you may make mistakes while developing it.
Instead of directly changing the working code on main, you can create a separate branch.
main → Working website ✅ \ \ feature-login → Build login feature 🚧
You can work on feature-login without directly changing the code on main.
Simple Real-World Example
Suppose your project currently has these files:
main │ ├── index.html ├── style.css └── script.js Website working ✅
You now want to add a login page.
Create a branch for the feature:
main │ └── feature-login
Then make your changes in the new branch:
main Website working version ✅ feature-login ├── Add login.html ├── Add login CSS └── Add login JavaScript
The development work happens separately until you decide the feature is ready.
What Does "Separate Line of Development" Mean?
Suppose your project has three commits.
Commit A → Create project ↓ Commit B → Add homepage ↓ Commit C → Add navigation ↓ main
At this point, you create a new branch called feature-login.
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C │ main │ └── feature-login
Both branches initially point to the same project history. After you start making commits on the new branch, their histories can develop separately.
Branch Development Example
Commit D → Add login page feature-login ↗ / Commit A → Commit B → Commit C \ main ↓ Working code remains unchanged
Now:

BranchState
mainContains the original working project
feature-loginContains the new login feature work
The Main Idea 🧠
A branch lets you experiment or build a feature safely.
main ↓ Stable code ✅ Create branch ↓ feature-new ↓ Try new changes 🧪 ↓ If successful → Merge later If unsuccessful → main is still unaffected
This separation is one of the biggest advantages of branches.
Branch Names
A branch has a name so Git can identify it.
Examples:
main feature-login feature-dashboard fix-login-bug update-homepage
Branch names should clearly describe the purpose of the work.
Good names ✅ feature-login fix-payment-bug update-dashboard -------------------- Unclear names ⚠️ branch1 newbranch test123
main Branch
Most repositories have a primary branch commonly named main.
You can think of it as the main line of development.
main ↓ Main project development ↓ Often contains stable code
Other branches are usually created from an existing branch and are later merged when their work is ready.
Important: main is just a branch name. Git does not technically treat it as a magical or special type of branch; it is commonly used as the primary branch name.
Branches and Commits
Branches work together with commits.
Create branch ↓ Make changes ↓ git add ↓ git commit ↓ Branch gets new commit history
A branch itself is not the same as a commit.

ConceptMeaning
CommitA saved snapshot in Git history
BranchA named line that points through a sequence of commits
Simple Analogy 📚
Imagine you are writing a book.
Main Book Version ↓ Working manuscript 📘
You want to try a completely different ending.
Main Version 📘 │ └── Alternative Ending Draft ✏️
You can write and test the alternative ending without destroying the original manuscript.
A Git branch works in a similar way: it gives you a separate path for development.
Multiple Branches Example
A project can have multiple branches at the same time.
feature-login / main ──────────── feature-dashboard \ fix-payment-bug
Different features or fixes can be developed independently.

BranchPurpose
mainMain project code
feature-loginDevelop login feature
feature-dashboardDevelop dashboard feature
fix-payment-bugFix a payment problem
Important: Creating a Branch Does Not Automatically Change Branches
This is important for the next topics.
You can create a branch, but Git may keep you on your current branch depending on the command you use.
Currently on: main ↓ Create feature-login branch ↓ feature-login exists ✅ ↓ But you may still be working on main
You will learn the exact commands for creating and switching branches in the upcoming topics.
Branch Workflow
main Stable project ✅ ↓ Create feature branch ↓ feature-login ↓ Make changes ↓ Test changes ↓ Create commits ↓ Feature completed ↓ Merge into main ↓ main contains new feature ✅
What Happens After the Feature Is Complete?
After the work in a branch is finished and tested, you can combine it with another branch using merge.
main Commit A → Commit B \ feature-login Commit C → Commit D ↓ Merge ↓ main now includes login feature ✅
You will learn merging in detail later. For now, remember that branches allow separate development and merging combines development histories.
Branch vs Repository
These two concepts are different.

ConceptMeaning
RepositoryThe complete Git project containing files and history
BranchA separate line of development inside the repository
Repository 📁 │ ├── main branch │ ├── feature-login branch │ └── fix-bug branch
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
Repository → The complete project Commit → A saved point in history Branch → A separate development path Merge → Combine branch work
Complete Example

START ↓ main Website is working ✅ ↓ Need new login feature ↓ Create feature-login branch ↓ Work independently 🚧 ↓ Add login page ↓ Add validation ↓ Commit changes ↓ Test feature ↓ Merge into main ↓ main now contains the feature ✅
One-Line Definition: A Git branch is an independent line of development that allows you to work on features, fixes, or experiments separately without directly affecting another branch such as main.
practice: For this first branch topic, focus mainly on understanding the concept. The next topics will teach you the commands to create, switch, list, and delete branches.
SCENARIO ↓ main → Website is working ✅ ↓ You need to add a login feature ↓ Would you change main directly? 🤔 ↓ Create a separate branch ↓ feature-login 🚧 ↓ Develop safely ↓ Merge later when ready
Practice Task 1: Imagine your current website is working correctly on the main branch. Write down three features that you might develop in separate branches.
Example: feature-login feature-dashboard fix-navigation-bug
Practice Task 2: For each situation below, decide whether creating a separate branch would be useful.
1. Adding a completely new payment feature 2. Experimenting with a new homepage design 3. Fixing a serious login bug 4. Adding a dashboard Think: Could this work be developed separately from main?
Practice Task 3: Understand this history before moving to the next topic.
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C │ main │ └── feature-login
Both branches can initially start from the same commit. After new commits are created on one branch, their development can become different.
Practice Goal: Clearly understand that a branch is a separate line of development. You do not need to memorize branch commands yet because those are covered in the next topics.

qna.q: Q1. What is a branch in Git?
qna.a: A branch is an independent line of development where you can make changes separately from another branch.

qna.q: Q2. Why are branches useful?
qna.a: Branches allow you to develop features, fix bugs, or experiment with changes without directly affecting the main line of development.

qna.q: Q3. What is main?
qna.a: main is commonly used as the primary branch of a repository. It is a branch name, not a special type of Git object.

qna.q: Q4. Is a branch the same as a commit?
qna.a: No. A commit is a saved snapshot in Git history, while a branch represents a named line of development through commits.

qna.q: Q5. Can a repository have multiple branches?
qna.a: Yes. A repository can have multiple branches for different features, bug fixes, experiments, or other development work.

qna.q: Q6. Give an example of a useful branch name.
qna.a: Examples include feature-login, feature-dashboard, fix-payment-bug, and update-homepage.

qna.q: Q7. What is the main benefit of developing a feature in a separate branch?
qna.a: You can work on the feature independently without directly changing the code on the main branch.

qna.q: Q8. What can happen after work on a branch is completed?
qna.a: The completed and tested work can be merged into another branch, such as main.

qna.q: Q9. Does creating a branch automatically mean you are now working on that branch?
qna.a: Not necessarily. Creating and switching branches are separate concepts depending on the command used.

qna.q: Q10. Repository vs Branch — what is the difference?
qna.a: A repository is the complete Git project containing files and history, while a branch is a separate line of development inside that repository.

items.title: Why Branches Are Used
explanation: Simple Meaning
Branches are used to work on different features, bug fixes, or experiments separately without directly affecting the main working code.
main ↓ Working project ✅ Need a new feature ↓ Create separate branch ↓ Work independently 🚧 ↓ Test changes ↓ Merge when ready
Simple Rule: Use branches when you want to make changes separately and keep the main code safe from unfinished work.
Main Problem Without Branches
Imagine your website is working correctly and all your work is directly done on main.
main ↓ Website working perfectly ✅ ↓ Start building a new feature ↓ Modify existing files directly ↓ Feature is unfinished 🚧 ↓ Something breaks ❌ ↓ main is now affected
This can make development risky because unfinished or experimental changes are mixed with your main project code.
Solution: Use a Branch
Instead of directly working on main, create a separate branch for the work.
main Working project ✅ │ ├── feature-login 🚧 │ └── fix-navbar-bug 🛠️
Each piece of work can be developed independently. The main branch remains unchanged until you intentionally merge the completed work.
Reason 1: Develop New Features Safely ⭐
This is one of the most common reasons for using branches.
Suppose your website is live and working:
main ↓ Homepage ✅ Login ✅ Dashboard ✅
Now you want to add a payment feature that may require many changes.
main Working project ✅ │ └── feature-payment ↓ Add payment page ↓ Add validation ↓ Test feature ↓ Ready? → Merge into main
The unfinished payment work stays separate until it is ready.
Reason 2: Keep main Stable ⭐
A common workflow is to keep main as stable as possible.
main ↓ Stable code ✅ -------------------- feature-login ↓ New development 🚧 -------------------- fix-payment-bug ↓ Bug fix 🛠️
You can make many commits while developing on another branch without those commits changing the current code on main.
Important: Changes from one branch are not added to another branch automatically. You normally combine branch work intentionally using operations such as merging.
Reason 3: Work on Multiple Things at the Same Time
Projects often need multiple pieces of work at the same time.
Repository │ ├── main │ Stable project ✅ │ ├── feature-login │ New login feature 🚧 │ ├── feature-dashboard │ New dashboard 🚧 │ └── fix-navbar-bug Bug fix 🛠️
Branches help organize these different tasks so their development histories can remain separate.
Example: One Developer
Branches are useful even when you are working alone.
You are working alone 👤 ↓ main → Working website ↓ Create feature-dark-mode ↓ Experiment with dark mode ↓ Test it ↓ If good → Merge If not good → Do not merge
You do not need a team to benefit from branches.
Reason 4: Experiment Without Affecting Main
Sometimes you want to try an idea but you are not sure whether it will work.
main ↓ Current design ✅ │ └── experiment-new-design ↓ Try different layout 🧪 ↓ Try new colors ↓ Try different navigation ↓ Decide later
If the experiment is successful, you can later integrate it. If you do not want the experiment, your main branch remains unchanged by those branch commits.
Reason 5: Fix Bugs Separately
Branches are also useful for bug fixes.
main ↓ Website working ↓ Login bug discovered 🐛 ↓ Create fix-login-bug branch ↓ Investigate problem ↓ Fix code ↓ Test fix ↓ Merge fix into main
A clear branch name also makes the purpose of the work easier to understand.
fix-login-bug
Reason 6: Separate Unfinished Work
Some features take several hours, days, or even weeks to complete.
Day 1 → Start feature Day 2 → Add some code Day 3 → Find a problem Day 4 → Continue development Day 5 → Test feature Day 6 → Feature complete
Instead of mixing all this unfinished development directly into the main project line, you can keep it on a feature branch until it is ready.
main → Stable version ✅ feature-new → Day 1 🚧 Day 2 🚧 Day 3 🚧 Day 4 🚧 Day 5 🚧 Day 6 Complete ✅
Reason 7: Easier Code Review
In a team, a branch can represent one specific piece of work.
feature-login ↓ Only login-related changes ↓ Review changes ↓ Check code ↓ Test feature ↓ Merge when approved
This makes it easier to understand what a set of changes is intended to do compared with mixing many unrelated changes together.
Example: Team Workflow
main Stable project │ ├── Developer A │ └── feature-login │ ↓ │ Builds login feature │ ├── Developer B │ └── feature-dashboard │ ↓ │ Builds dashboard │ └── Developer C └── fix-payment-bug ↓ Fixes bug
Each developer can work on a separate task. When the work is ready, it can be reviewed and integrated into the main development line according to the team's workflow.
Reason 8: Organize Project Development
Branches can make the purpose of different development work clear.

BranchPurpose
mainMain project development
feature-loginDevelop login feature
feature-searchDevelop search feature
fix-payment-bugFix payment problem
experiment-uiTest a UI idea

Without BranchesWith Branches
All work happens directly on mainWork can be separated by task
Unfinished work can mix with stable codeUnfinished work can remain on a feature branch
Experiments directly affect the current branchExperiments can be developed separately
Multiple tasks become harder to organizeFeatures and fixes can have separate branches

Important Example
Imagine your project has two urgent tasks:
Task 1 → Add new dashboard feature 🚧 Task 2 → Fix critical login bug 🐛
Using branches, you could organize the work like this:
main │ ├── feature-dashboard │ ↓ │ Continue developing dashboard │ └── fix-login-bug ↓ Fix and test login bug
The two tasks can have separate commits and histories instead of being mixed into one line of development.
Branch Does Not Mean a Copy of the Entire Project
For beginners, it is useful to avoid thinking of every branch as manually creating a completely separate folder containing a full project copy.
Conceptually, a branch is a separate line of development through Git's commit history.
Commit A → Commit B → Commit C │ main │ └── feature-login ↓ Commit D → Commit E
Git manages this history efficiently. The important concept for now is that commits can develop differently after branches diverge.
Most Common Branch Workflow
1. main Stable code ✅ ↓ 2. Create feature branch ↓ 3. Work on feature ↓ 4. Create commits ↓ 5. Test changes ↓ 6. Review changes ↓ 7. Merge into main ↓ 8. main updated with completed feature ✅
Real Example: Adding a Search Feature

START ↓ main → Website working ✅ ↓ Need search feature ↓ Create feature-search ↓ Add search input ↓ Add search logic ↓ Fix problems ↓ Create commits ↓ Test feature ↓ Feature ready ↓ Merge into main ↓ Website now includes search ✅
When You Should Think About Creating a Branch
Ask yourself:

Am I adding a new feature? → Probably create a branch Am I fixing a bug? → A separate branch can be useful Am I testing an idea? → A separate branch is useful Am I making a large change? → A separate branch is useful Am I working on a separate task? → Consider a branch
The exact branching workflow can vary between projects and teams, but the core purpose remains separation of development work.
Easy Way to Remember 🧠
main → Main/stable development line feature branch → Build something new bug-fix branch → Fix a problem experiment branch → Try an idea Merge → Intentionally combine completed work

qna.q: Q1. What is the main reason branches are used?
qna.a: Branches are used to separate development work so features, bug fixes, and experiments can be developed without directly mixing unfinished changes into the main line of development.

qna.q: Q2. Why should you avoid doing all unfinished work directly on main?
qna.a: Because unfinished or experimental changes can mix with the main project code and make the main development line less stable.

qna.q: Q3. Are branches useful only for teams?
qna.a: No. Branches are useful for both individual developers and teams.

qna.q: Q4. Give three common reasons to create a branch.
qna.a: Common reasons include developing a new feature, fixing a bug, and experimenting with a new idea.

qna.q: Q5. What is the benefit of a feature branch?
qna.a: It allows a new feature to be developed and tested separately before it is intentionally integrated into another branch such as main.

qna.q: Q6. Can multiple tasks have separate branches?
qna.a: Yes. For example, feature-login, feature-dashboard, and fix-payment-bug can all be separate branches.

qna.q: Q7. If you create commits on a feature branch, are those changes automatically added to main?
qna.a: No. Branch changes are not automatically added to main. They must be intentionally integrated using an appropriate Git operation such as merging.

qna.q: Q8. Why are branches useful for experiments?
qna.a: They allow you to try changes on a separate line of development without directly adding the experimental commits to main.

qna.q: Q9. How can branches help a team?
qna.a: Different developers can work on separate features or bug fixes with separate branches, making the work easier to organize and review.

qna.q: Q10. What should you remember before learning branch commands?
qna.a: Branches are mainly used to separate development work, keep tasks organized, allow safer experimentation, and integrate completed work when appropriate.
